top_choice_rationale: Optical lattice clocks rest on a clean physical idea, the magic wavelength at which the trap shifts both clock levels equally, and on the kind of verification I trust most: independent clocks in several countries agree at the 1e-18 level. The Katori and Ye credit maps onto the invention and the demonstrated record performance, and it fits the laureate limit without painful omissions. I weigh the novelty objection from the 2005 and 2012 prizes and my own bias toward atomic physics, so I rank magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene second. It is a legitimate and strong case, a quantitative prediction followed by a sharp experimental test and wide reproduction, but the third seat, the open pairing mechanism and the device dependence leave it less closed to me. No award is last because both proposals describe real, reproduced achievements.
recusal_note: Long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier and close to the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, and works in atomic physics adjacent to the clock field. I have no apparent direct tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Bistritzer or Jarillo-Herrero from the profile, but a recusal check for the atomic-physics proposal might be considered.
